source: (1) Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes, David Rein, 'Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity', arXiv:2507.09089 (v1 12 Jul 2025, v2 25 Jul 2025), METR. Opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089 and full text https://arxiv.org/html/2507.09089v2. (2) Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud, 'We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design', METR blog, February 24, 2026. Opened: https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/
data_type: RCT (task-level randomisation, self-reported task times plus screen recordings) for the 2025 paper; the 2026 update reports raw results of a second task-randomised RCT plus participant surveys and interviews.
sample_and_method: 2025 paper: 16 experienced open-source developers 'with moderate AI experience' completed 246 tasks in mature projects where they averaged 5 years of prior experience (about 1,500 commits each to the repo). Repositories averaged 23,000 stars and 1,100,000 lines of code. Recruited from METR's professional networks and outreach to active contributors to large GitHub repos; paid $150/hour. Developers pre-specified issues, each issue randomly assigned AI-allowed or AI-disallowed; tools mostly Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet; fieldwork February to June 2025. Screen recordings collected; 128 recordings (143 hours) labelled at fine grain, with a filtered subset of 74 issues used for activity analysis. 2026 update: second study started August 2025 with 10 developers from the original study plus 47 new developers from 'a more diverse set of open-source projects' (smaller, more greenfield, less mature repos), median 10 years experience, paid $50/hour; 'We have data from 57 developers, across 143 repos, and 800+ tasks.'
vendor_interest: No. METR is a nonprofit studying frontier AI agents and does not sell AI or measurement tooling. Its stated interest is AI R&D acceleration and risk. The 2025 study provided Cursor Pro subscriptions but was not vendor funded as far as the pages state.
headline_figures: 2025 abstract: 'Before starting tasks, developers forecast that allowing AI will reduce completion time by 24%. After completing the study, developers estimate that allowing AI reduced completion time by 20%. Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%--AI tooling slowed developers down. This slowdown also contradicts predictions from experts in economics (39% shorter) and ML (38% shorter).' Paper factor table: 'Developers accept 44% of AI generations' and '9% of time spent reviewing/cleaning AI outputs'. Paper: 'developers write 47% (p = 0.16) more code per hour of AI-disallowed forecasts, on issues where AI is allowed. This is not statistically significant'. 2026 update: 'Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%. For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.' (In METR's sign convention here a negative figure means less time taken, i.e. a speedup.) 'When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.'
metric_layer: Activity/output at task level: wall-clock time to complete a developer-defined issue (self-reported time, checked against screen recordings), plus perceived speedup (forecast and post-hoc self-estimate). Some input/usage data (Cursor accepted lines, activity labels). Quality is held roughly constant by repository review standards but not measured as an outcome; no delivery or financial layer.
respondent_role_split: Not applicable. All participants are individual open-source contributors (ICs); no manager, director or executive split. The 2026 update splits only by returning (original) versus newly recruited developers.
workload_signal: 2025 paper: with AI allowed, developers spent less time actively coding and reading, and more time 'reviewing AI outputs, prompting AI systems, and waiting for AI generations', plus 'a somewhat higher proportion of their time idle'; 9% of time spent reviewing/cleaning AI outputs; majority reported making major changes to clean up AI code. 2026 update: developers using agents 'would often work an unrelated task while waiting for the agent to complete its work', making time-spent hard to report; one developer described working without AI as 'trying to get across the city walking when all of a sudden I was more used to taking an Uber.' No hours, burnout or pressure-to-use measures.
definition_of_value_offered: Implicitly yes: value is defined as reduction in time to complete a fixed, pre-specified real task with quality held to the repository's normal bar, measured by randomisation rather than self-report. The paper's design rationale is that self-reported and forecast speedups are unreliable (devs believed 20% faster while measured 19% slower). The 2026 update argues this measure is now 'likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact' because task selection, task-type substitution and quality differences mean 'the time-differences within the study may not represent value-differences'. It lists alternatives: shorter intensive experiments, observational data, questionnaires with time-use studies, fixed-task experiments, agent evals, and developer-level randomisation.
removal_counterfactual: The AI-disallowed arm is a removal condition. In 2025 removing AI made tasks faster on average (AI-allowed took 19% longer). By 2026 the removal condition itself drove attrition: 'developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI'; 'An increased share of developers say they would not want to do 50% of their work without AI'; '30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI. This implies we are systematically missing tasks which have high expected uplift from AI.' Also: 'Some developers were less likely to complete tasks that they submitted if they were assigned to the AI-disallowed condition. One developer did not complete any of the tasks that were assigned to the AI-disallowed condition.' METR concludes its estimate is 'a lower-bound on the true productivity effects' but its data 'is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.'
key_quotes: 1. 'Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%--AI tooling slowed developers down.' (arXiv abstract) 2. 'I avoid issues like AI can finish things in just 2 hours, but I have to spend 20 hours. I will feel so painful if the task is decided as AI-disallowed.' (developer quoted in METR 2026 update)
caveats: Small 2025 sample (16 developers) of highly experienced devs in large mature repos; paper explicitly says it does not show AI fails to speed up most developers. 2026 raw estimates have confidence intervals crossing zero and are biased by selection (developer opt-out, task withholding, pay cut from $150 to $50/hour, multi-agent time-tracking problems, task substitution, quality differences). Withholding figure (30% to 50%) is survey self-report. Figure conflict within the 2026 post itself: its opening sentence says the earlier paper 'found the use of AI tools caused a 20% slowdown', while later the same post and the paper abstract say 19% longer; 19% is the paper's figure (20% is the developers' post-hoc perceived speedup). Self-reported speedups described by METR as 'quite unreliable'.
access: Primary sources opened in full: arXiv abstract page, arXiv HTML full text v2 (searched for specific passages, not read line by line), and the full METR 2026 blog post. All quotes taken verbatim from downloaded page text. Not verified: the underlying datasets linked from the blog; the companion METR survey of 349 technical workers (only seen as a teaser on the page, not opened).
